prompt: Where do iOS and macOS get their Swift compiler from?
hint: They were not on swift.org's list for 6.4.2.

choices.text: From a separate Swift language made for Apple devices
choices.why: It is the same language and the same release number.

choices.text: From the Ubuntu 24.04 archive
choices.why: Ubuntu does not even package Swift for Linux.

choices.text: From the Static SDK on swift.org's list
choices.why: That SDK builds for Linux, with musl.

choices.text: From Xcode
choices.why: Right: Apple's platforms get their Swift inside Xcode, or the Command Line Tools.

prompt: What is a Swift SDK such as the Wasm SDK, as opposed to the Ubuntu 24.04 entry on the list?
hint: The third command of the section listed them.

choices.text: Xcode's version for Linux
choices.why: There is no Xcode for Linux.

choices.text: A complete toolchain for another operating system
choices.why: Those are the Linux and Windows entries; an SDK has no compiler of its own.

choices.text: A plugin that adds new syntax to the language
choices.why: The language is the same for every target.

choices.text: A bundle for building for another target
choices.why: Right: libraries and settings for a target other than the machine you are on.

prompt: A team wants the planner's model code, written in Swift, to run inside an Android app whose screens are in Kotlin. Which entry of the list is about that?
hint: What the section said the Android entry is, and is not.

choices.text: Embedded Swift
choices.why: That mode is for microcontrollers, and is not an entry on the list.

choices.text: The static Linux SDK, since Android runs Linux
choices.why: A static Linux binary is a program to start, not a library inside an Android app.

choices.text: None: Swift cannot leave Apple's platforms
choices.why: The list itself shows Linux, Windows and three SDKs.

choices.text: The Android SDK
choices.why: Right: it builds Android libraries from Swift, while the screens stay in Kotlin.

prompt: On Linux, which module has to be imported to use `URLSession`?

choices.text: `FoundationNetworking`
choices.why: Right: on Linux networking is a separate module, built on libcurl.

choices.text: `Hummingbird`
choices.why: Hummingbird is a server framework; the client in section 04 did not import it.

choices.text: `Darwin`
choices.why: `Darwin` exists only on Apple's systems.

choices.text: `Glibc`
choices.why: That is the C library underneath, and it has no `URLSession`.

prompt: Why does `#if canImport(FoundationNetworking)` beat `#if os(Linux)` around that import?
hint: What does the code actually need?

choices.text: `os(Linux)` does not exist in Swift 6
choices.why: `Where.swift` used it and printed "Compiled for Linux".

choices.text: They are the same check spelt two ways
choices.why: One names a system, the other a module; they differ on Windows.

choices.text: `os(Linux)` is checked while the program runs, which is too late
choices.why: Both conditions are decided at compile time.

choices.text: It asks about the module itself
choices.why: Right: Windows has the module too, and a test on one system's name would miss it.

prompt: A file built on Linux contains `#elseif os(macOS)` followed by a call to a function Linux does not have. What does the compiler do with that line?

choices.text: Warns, and replaces the call with a stub that does nothing
choices.why: Nothing is replaced; the line is simply absent from the build.

choices.text: Refuses it: the function cannot be found
choices.why: The line is dropped before it is checked.

choices.text: Compiles it, and the program crashes if it reaches that line
choices.why: It is not compiled at all, so it can never be reached.

choices.text: Drops it before checking it
choices.why: Right: a branch not taken is not compiled, so it may name anything.

prompt: Apple's other frameworks, such as SwiftUI, UIKit and ___, are not available on Linux at all; `Where.swift` checked one of them with `canImport`.
hint: A framework for values over time, named in the section's list.

prompt: In the Hummingbird server, what turned the array of `Session` into JSON?

choices.text: `Session` conforms to `ResponseCodable`
choices.why: Right: `Codable`, plus Hummingbird's promise to send the value as JSON.

choices.text: A `JSONEncoder` the route created by hand
choices.why: The route only returned `sessions`.

choices.text: `curl`, which formats what it receives
choices.why: `curl` prints the bytes the server sent.

choices.text: SwiftNIO converts every struct it sees
choices.why: SwiftNIO moves bytes; the conformance decides the encoding.

prompt: What HTTP status did the server answer for `/semana`, a path no route handles?
Why does the section run the server in one terminal and `curl` in a second one?

choices.text: The server runs until it is stopped
choices.why: Right: `runService` returns only when the server stops, with Ctrl+C.

choices.text: Port 8090 belongs to the first terminal
choices.why: A port belongs to a process, and any terminal on the machine can reach it.

choices.text: `swift run` stops the server when the build ends
choices.why: The server outlived the build and answered three requests.

choices.text: `curl` refuses to talk to a process in the same terminal
choices.why: It does not know or care which terminal the server is in.

prompt: Someone renames `minutes` to `duration` in the server's `Session` and leaves `Client.swift` alone. What happens when the client runs?

choices.text: Decoding fails with `keyNotFound` for `minutes`
choices.why: Right: the client still asks for `minutes`, and one shared model package would have caught it at build time.

choices.text: `minutes` decodes as 0
choices.why: A non-optional `Int` has no default when its key is missing.

choices.text: Nothing changes: JSON keys come from the client's struct
choices.why: The keys come from whoever encoded the JSON, the server.

choices.text: The server refuses to compile until the client is updated
choices.why: Nothing links the two files; that is the problem.

prompt: Which C library does the static Linux SDK link into the executable?

choices.text: None: a static binary calls no C library
choices.why: It calls one, and carries it inside.

choices.text: glibc, from Ubuntu
choices.why: glibc is what the dynamic build uses; the static SDK replaces it.

choices.text: Darwin
choices.why: Darwin is Apple's.

choices.text: musl
choices.why: Right: a small C library written to be linked statically.

prompt: On the machine with no Swift, `./week-dynamic` failed. What did the message name?
hint: The same loader message as lesson 1.

choices.text: A missing `swift` command
choices.why: The binary never calls `swift`.

choices.text: `libswiftCore.so`
choices.why: Right: the runtime it borrows from the toolchain each time it starts.

choices.text: A wrong processor architecture
choices.why: Both machines were x86-64; the static binary ran there.

choices.text: A bad checksum
choices.why: The checksum belonged to the SDK download, not to this binary.

prompt: Which of these does the statically linked `week` carry inside it? Choose all that apply.

choices.text: A C library
choices.why: Yes: musl.

choices.text: The Swift compiler
choices.why: No: a binary carries no compiler.

choices.text: Ubuntu's glibc
choices.why: No: musl replaces it.

choices.text: The Swift runtime
choices.why: Yes: that is what the dynamic one looks for in the toolchain.

prompt: A colleague's servers are 64-bit ARM machines running Linux. What do you build the planner server with?
hint: The same bundle has more than one target.

choices.text: The Android SDK, which targets ARM
choices.why: It builds Android libraries, not a Linux server.

choices.text: Xcode, which builds for ARM by default on a recent Mac
choices.why: That produces Mac programs, not Linux ones.

choices.text: The x86-64 static binary, which runs on any Linux
choices.why: Any Linux distribution, on the same processor family.

choices.text: `--swift-sdk aarch64-swift-linux-musl`
choices.why: Right: the static SDK carries an aarch64 target beside the x86-64 one.

prompt: Why was nothing in the section on the Mac run for this course?

choices.text: Xcode costs money to download
choices.why: Price was not the reason the section gives.

choices.text: Swift is not allowed to run on a Mac
choices.why: A Mac is Swift's oldest home.

choices.text: The commands of this course would not work there
choices.why: They would, as written; paths and a few lines of output would differ.

choices.text: The course was recorded with no Mac
choices.why: Right: Apple's tools run only on Apple hardware, and there was none.

prompt: A student has no Mac and wants to follow `ios-apps`. Which statement about hosted build services is true, according to this lesson?
hint: What do they give, and what do they leave out?

choices.text: They replace Xcode with a Linux build of it
choices.why: They still run Xcode, on somebody else's Mac.

choices.text: They build and sign, with no simulator
choices.why: Right: building is solved; developing against a simulator on your own screen is not.

choices.text: They let SwiftUI be imported on Linux
choices.why: SwiftUI stays an Apple framework.

choices.text: They are free and need no account
choices.why: The section says companies rent these by the hour.

prompt: Which part of the planner carries over to `ios-apps` as code, not only as knowledge?

choices.text: The model layer
choices.why: Right: none of it imports Apple's frameworks, so it compiles there unchanged.

choices.text: The Hummingbird server
choices.why: The server runs on Linux and is not part of the iPhone app.

choices.text: The static binary
choices.why: It runs on Linux only.

choices.text: The screens
choices.why: The screens are SwiftUI, which `ios-apps` adds.

prompt: A Mac-written file using `URLSession` is copied to Linux. What fixes it so that it still compiles on both?

choices.text: The import inside `#if canImport(FoundationNetworking)`
choices.why: Right: on Linux the module exists and is imported, and on a Mac the line is dropped.

choices.text: Replacing `URLSession` with `curl` called through a shell
choices.why: That is a different program, and the fix is one import.

choices.text: `import FoundationNetworking` on its own
choices.why: That line breaks the Mac build, where the module does not exist.

choices.text: Building it with the static Linux SDK
choices.why: The static SDK still needs the import.
